utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you gave at the beginning of your evidence still applies, Mr. Panic. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an intervention regarding the transcript. I have a minor correction concerning the translation, but I will verify this during the break. And I will bring it up in the next session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, good morning. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. We will continue where we left off yesterday, but let me ask you something I may have failed to ask you yesterday. You said that before going to the cabinet session, you saw a bus in the barracks, and you described the situation that was taking place in front of the bus. Yesterday, you said that there was no mention of any buses going -- of anyone going either to Ovcara or to barracks when the triage was discussed. So were you surprised, what was your reaction when you say that bus? What did you conclude?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no mention of buses with the people from the hospital coming to the barracks, because the barracks was being prepared for quite a different activity that was to take place on the following day. This is why I was surprised when I saw a bus there. It drew my attention so I approached it. I saw the people on the bus and I saw other people trying to approach the bus, but they were prevented from approaching by the military police unit which was in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you inform anyone about the fact that you saw this bus before going to the cabinet session and, if so, whom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following that when Commander Mrksic called me and told me to go to the cabinet session, I mentioned to him that there was already a bus -- one bus in the barracks, and that there were people trying to approach the bus in order to recognise someone who may have harmed their family members. So the conclusion is yes, I informed Colonel Mrksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, we adjourned at -- when we discussed the cabinet session. But we are now about to see a video excerpt but let me first ask you this: While you were at the cabinet session, did you see Veselin Sljivancanin coming there or his deputy Ljubisa Vukasinovic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see either one of them, either before or after the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that means during the session also?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from anyone that he may have dropped in?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody mentioned him at this session. And while I stayed there briefly, nobody mentioned him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We are now going to see a video excerpt. Your Honours, I believe it's video 269. Mr. Panic, if you recognise someone, please tell us and we'll try to identify it by reference to the time indication on the video excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see it on your screen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could somebody please ensure that Mr. Panic has it on his screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see it now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see it now? Do you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is 07:03 time reference, who did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognised Goran Hadzic and Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is 07:07. Can you recognise anyone now on this frame?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it any longer. This is Arkan. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We anyway proceed.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Hadzic and then Dusan Jaksic, commander of the Territorial Defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is 07:17. Is this still him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, still Dusan Jaksic. He is now kissing someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise anyone here?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the colonel here; the one who attended the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please rewind just a little bit. Stop now please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A person wearing a cap, Tito-style cap is the colonel who attended the cabinet session. At the time, I didn't know his name. I didn't know him at all. And it wasn't until many years later, once the Ovcara trial started, that I had occasion to meet him at the special court in Belgrade. This is Bogdan Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are now at 07:34. Since there are several faces here, could you be more specific. Which one is him on this freeze-frame?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in front of me -- well, I have it now. Yes, I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you please describe ...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the man on the left of the screen; he is facing us. He has a Tito-style cap on his head. We can see most of his face; definitely his nose and his right eye and the rest is -- the rest of it is obstructed by this other person standing in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We may proceed. That's it. We don't need to play it any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, what happened afterwards, after the meeting, after the cabinet session that you attended?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After attending the cabinet session, I returned to the barracks; and then I saw two or three additional two or three buses at the barracks. I think that people from the hospital were on the buses, at least that's what I was told, and there were guards securing the buses. The situation was a bit more calm. There were fewer curious people than in the case of the first bus that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you happen to see any trucks or any ambulance vehicles next to the buses?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see any other vehicles; I only saw the policemen standing there and securing the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the barracks, the building where there is a telephone, the same telephone via which I received my order. And I informed Colonel Mrksic that I had attended the cabinet session, that the session was over, that there was a heated debate, that the JNA was insulted there, and I don't need to go into details unless you ask me to. I simply described the situation at the session. I described it briefly, and I said that they had decided that they were going to put these criminals, as they called them, on trial. Criminals from the hospital that they said that they wouldn't allow for them to be transported to Mitrovica. And if they failed to prevent us in transporting them, they were ready to lay down on the road and we would have to drive over their bodies. That was the last option.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us just be more specific. You said "they said" who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the conclusion reached at the cabinet session. This is something uttered by Goran Hadzic. And they said that there would be a prison at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Mrksic just made brief comments saying: "Very well, let it be as they decided."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How much longer did you stay at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed for another couple of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see the moment when the buses left the barracks? Were you present on the premises or within the compound?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't present. But later, when I left, as I had to go to Negoslavci, there were no longer any buses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, during that period of time, that is to say in the morning from the moment when you came to the barracks for the first time until you left the barracks, did you see Mr. Sljivancanin in the barracks at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw him in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from anyone that he may have dropped in, that he may have come to the barracks during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear that and I didn't see him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is not a speculative question, rather, it is more of a theoretical nature. If chief of security had known that you, as Chief of Staff, were in the barracks, would he have expected you to come in and talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only him, but other officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object to that. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The objection is upheld, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I put the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is not being allowed. We will not take notice of the answer. How can this witness say what others would have thought or done?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a theoretical question. I wanted to inquire about the procedure. Perhaps I didn't phrase it well, but I think that the witness is competent to explain what a typical procedure is. And by your leave, I would put such a question to him because he is a senior officer. It's not a factual question; I'm just interested in establishing what the regular procedure was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question as to the normal procedure will be allowed, Mr. Lukic, but your question was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, within the system of singleness of command, within the system that existed in the JNA, on any premises, if the Chief of Staff of a unit is present, as is his subordinate officer, do they have a duty of reporting to each other?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a regular procedure. This is something mandated by regulations both in peacetime, and especially during wartime when there is both a desire and a need to meet and exchange information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened then, Mr. Panic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my stay at the barracks and after I worked on the tasks that I had received in relation to preparing the press conference for the following day, I went out into the compound of the barracks, where my driver was waiting with the vehicle, and I set out to Negoslavci to the command post of Operations Group South. Since I still had some time left, in terms of daytime, that is, it was sometime in the afternoon, I decided to stop by at Ovcara. Ovcara is on the road between the barracks and our command post. I felt it necessary to see whether these people from the hospital were actually put up at Ovcara, to see whether the are authorities that made a decision at the session and concluded that they would be running a trial, to see whether they actually arrived on the spot and, quite simply, what was going on at Ovcara, so that when arriving at the command post, I would give more complete information about that to the commander. I reached Ovcara and I got to the hangar where members of military formations had been staying before, those who had already been transported to Mitrovica. On the road, I saw a few armed men, small groups of men. There were a few without weapons, too. There were people who were simply going up and down that road between Ovcara and Grabovo. Some even stayed by the hangar and tried to approach the entrance into the hangar. By the hangar, there was security; these were armed soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army. To be specific, or more specific, those were members of the 80th Motorised Brigade from their military police company, military policemen, that is. That is where I came across Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic, commander of the 80th Brigade. We exchanged a few words and he told me that there had been attempts made for those who were in front of the hangar and on the road or, rather, by them to enter the hangar and recognise someone. Quite simply, he said to me that he had the impression that some people were trying to take revenge, wanted to take revenge, but that he did not allow that and that his security did not allow that; the security that was in front of the hangar. I got to the entrance into the hangar, and I looked through the door. Since it's a big door, it's a farm, it was half closed. Perhaps there was just a metre or two. The door was ajar, and I saw the people who were standing in the hangar. It was a big group of people. They were throughout the hangar, but there were more of them in the other part and less of them near the door. There wasn't enough daylight there, because there is some small windows and openings there. In all fairness, I wasn't really interested in faces, but you could discern peoples's faces. I talked to Vojnovic a bit more there, and we concluded that the security needed to be stepped up so that there wouldn't be any undesired consequences. Bearing in mind the attempts made by these people from the road to approach the hangar, I did not stay there for a long time, perhaps ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you about a few details in relation to this part of your evidence. At that time, did you know who provided security during the night of the 18th for the Mitnica group at the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the procedure that was applied during the surrender of this Mitnica group. I've already commented upon that. It was done according to rules and in military fashion. The security was also provided by the police of the 80th Brigade, police security. I'm sorry. It's logical. It's their area of responsibility; it's a facility that is in their immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When talking to Vojnovic, when you concluded that perhaps security should be stepped up, did Vojinovic perhaps ask you to send some of your people from the Guards Brigade to help out, some security people?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not ask for any assistance because he had sufficient manpower. The 80th Brigade, not to go into its establishment and organisation, is a brigade that has a company of military police and many other units. In Ovcara itself, and in Grabovo, Jakupovac, and in other surrounding villages, they had battalion-level units that were strong enough to be used by him. Since combat activity was over, it was not logical for him to ask us for reinforcements. He did not ask for any.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, when you were at Ovcara, at that moment, did you see any people from the military police of the Guards Brigade there at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was not a single member there, except that I saw the buses that were turning around, passing by the hangar as they returned to where they had left from. I concluded that those were the buses that had brought those people in. Only in these buses, and that's what I saw in the barracks, too, there were military policemen. I can even remember that there were only two policemen in one bus; that is to say, in every bus, there were two policemen respectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me be very specific. These military policemen were on the buses that were leaving the area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses were leaving, and these policemen did not stay on the buses did not stay on. They turned around and they were going back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In that period while you were at Ovcara, did you see Veselin Sljivancanin at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him at Ovcara. I saw another officer, that was his deputy, Ljubisa Vukasinovic; however, Sljivancanin was not at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps talk to Vukasinovic? Do you remember what he was doing there, and where he was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just saw him briefly. He had some task; I don't know what it was. Perhaps he will be able to describe that. We didn't talk very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear from anyone that Sljivancanin was at Ovcara? Did Vojnovic perhaps mention that to you or Vukasinovic or anybody?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when talking to Vojnovic, did he express his surprise as to why those people were there? Did he say that he didn't want to provide security there, that he had nothing to do with that? Do you remember any such thing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As a matter of course, I saw him carrying out that assignment as he carried out his previous assignments. There was no need for me to doubt the seriousness of their implementation of that task, because he carried out the previous task as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you left Ovcara, what did Vojinovic and Vukasinovic do? Did they stay on there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed on. I already said that I was there very briefly, ten to 15 minutes, but the two of them stayed on. As a matter of fact, Vojnovic had his own command post in the immediate vicinity. That is where his command functioned. Vukasinovic stayed longer. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell us what happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From there, I returned to Negoslavci and at the command post, I found Colonel Mrksic. I briefed him in greater detail about everything that was going on, what I did, what I saw. Quite simply, he received complete information from me about all these things that I've been speaking about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This conversation of yours with Mr. Mrksic, was it during daytime, was it before the afternoon briefing? Can you define when it was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I went to Ovcara between 1400, 1500 hours, if I needed about ten to 15 minutes to stay there, or rather ten minutes to get there, too, I think it was about 1530 hours. It was daylight; you could still see properly. The subordinate commanders hadn't arrived yet or the command organs for the evening briefing. It was still the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you make any proposals to Colonel Mrksic then in relation to what was going on at the hangar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. When I informed him about all of this, I said it wouldn't be a bad thing if some of the security organs or military police went to Ovcara to indicate certain things or offer assistance, in professional terms, if necessary, to Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. I don't know whether he sent anyone. I think he did, and I think on the basis of everything I remember and having made these previous statements, too, I think that he actually did send some people there and I think that Mile Bozic was among them. He was there in Negoslavci at the command post or, rather, in a house there near the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From documents, we know that he was deputy commander of the village of Negoslavci, but, otherwise, what unit did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was from the 1st Battalion of the military police. And at first, while Kavalic was there as commander, he was his assistant commander for morale. After that, he became the deputy commander of that settlement. And I believe that since he was a policeman and since he was nearby, I think that Colonel Mrksic sent him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether the regular briefing took place on that day, and what was discussed there and whether any details were referred to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a regular briefing at that meeting, the regular meeting. I cannot say now whether everybody was present because there were quite a few parallel tasks on that day, and there were people who -- there were people who were outside our area of responsibility. Some were taking convoys of buses, some were involved in other work or this at the hospital, what was being done there, or the barracks. So my conclusion is that the meeting did take place, the meeting was attended by a majority, primarily of subordinate officers, and most of the members of the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember specifically whether Sljivancanin attended that meeting, whether he said something, whether he reported? Do you have any memory of that, and did you see him that evening at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, Sljivancanin was given time to say something at all meetings, to say things, to ask things. I don't remember that he was present, because I certainly would have remembered what it was that he would have said about what he did at the hospital. As far as I can remember, he came somewhat later to the command post. It was dark. In all fairness, at 1800 hours, it's dark, too. I think he came, say, around 2000 hours, and I know that he talked to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, from -- coming from Ovcara until the meeting held at the command post and later that evening -- actually, first of all, let me ask you, do you know who Borce Karanfilov is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At the time, I think he was a lieutenant, and he worked in the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember seeing him during that day at the command post, and did he actually ever come to the command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Karanfilov didn't come then to the command post, and I don't remember him coming earlier. There was really nothing for him to do at the command post. He had no business there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember your activities on the following day? Is there something that stands out on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the 21st of November because I was ordered and I was one of those people carrying out that order. The commander wasn't supposed to be there that day and a large group of journalists was expected, 100 to 120, both local and foreign journalists, and that was the main task for the 21st. We were supposed to greet them, take them to the barracks, enable them to organise a press conference, and ensure they are able to see a number of soldiers, commanders, regardless of all the trouble that we have had over the previous several days; as well as to see the others who took part in the liberation operation. I know that that morning, as soon as the commander left, and -- yes, that's another reason I remember the 21st; namely, because the commander and another group of people left for Belgrade. And they were supposed to attend a briefing and a reception given by Veljko Kadijevic, Federal Secretary for Defence. After they left for Belgrade, we set out towards the Vukovar barracks. And on that day, the press conference was held, as I have indicated. Following the press conference, the journalists were enabled to see Vukovar, to see the condition it was in, to meet with inhabitants, soldiers, officers, and so on, and they spent the entire day in Vukovar. This is why I remember the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When did the unit return to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our unit returned to Belgrade on the 24th; however, we received an order to be on standby, and we were ready to go back on a very short notice. We very actively worked on putting units from wartime disposition into peacetime disposition to let people rest, to organise vehicles, supplies, and so on. And we were expecting the order to return to come at any minute, but that didn't happen until the 24th when we returned to the garrison in Belgrade. We set out in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A question just occurred to me, and I don't really want us to look into the war diary. Do you remember in that period of time between the 21st and the 24th, were there various delegations of high officials, state officials coming to Vukovar, and did you meet them?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were delegations coming from state organs, civilian organs. There were quite a lot, and the largest majority of these delegations had to report to the commander. And given the level of dignitaries coming to visit, it was the commander who met with them and there were many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm mostly done, but let me put some questions to you because the OTP, when taking a statement from you, put some theoretical questions to you. Let me ask you, in professional terms, who can issue an order to a military police unit of the 80th Brigade to go to Ovcara and to secure the hangar there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the rules in force, the rules that were applied, a military police unit is under the command of its commander. Military police company is under the command of the company commander who receives his orders from his commander, that is to say, Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's say a military police company, who can issue an order to such a company to cease implementing its task and to withdraw?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logically speaking, such a task can be issued only by the unit's commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If anyone from superior command came to the area of responsibility of another unit without announcing their arrival, what would the commander of that area of responsibility be duty-bound to do? Would he need to verify some facts? What is the regular procedure under those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on our regulations, when somebody comes from a superior command, it is natural that he needs to be given full respect. And the commander needs to be informed that somebody has arrived to his area of responsibility. He knows who he receives his tasks from. He can obviously talk to the person who has arrived, but he previously needs to verify with his commander whether the person who has arrived is authorised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this a typical principle that exists within any army, whether singleness of command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a principle of singleness of command and unity of command. Ranks are respected, yes, but there are strict rules as to who is superior to whom and who is competent for what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, you spoke quite a lot about Mr. Sljivancanin giving your views, positions about him. Let me ask you to describe your impression of Veselin Sljivancanin, especially during the Vukovar operation in one sentence, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I answered a lot of OTP questions concerning the person of Major Sljivancanin at the time. In brief, Mr. Sljivancanin is a charismatic, imposing person who enjoyed great respect among his colleagues and subordinates, perhaps he stood out even more than necessary owing to his courage and his presence in all locations, where perhaps he did not necessarily have to be. I realised and I can explain that this has to do with a great desire on his part to carry out his tasks in the best possible manner, his eagerness to do that, as a result of which he perhaps received more high-profile attention than he should have or that corresponded to his position. He performed his duties conscientiously, wishing to ensure that his tasks are completed on time and in accordance with all existing regulations. I could speak about him at length.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you will have an opportunity to do so in cross-examination. Your Honours, I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Good morning, Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will be putting questions to you on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Mrksic. I may change the sequence of questions I have prepared for you, and I will do that in order to follow-up logically on the questions put to you by my colleague, Mr. Lukic. Please make a pause after hearing my question and I will do the same. We need to ensure the accuracy of the transcript. Towards the end of your examination-in-chief, you said that the company of military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade could only received its orders from company commander, and he could only receive his orders from brigade commander. Can the company commander and the company itself receive orders from any other officer pursuant -- who was authorised by the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such an order can be received, yes, but the company commander is duty to inform his commander and to ask his authorisation to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If the company commander of the military police commander to learn from his commander that a certain person is responsible for a certain task, does he still need to consult his commander about such a matter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, yes, especially under wartime, and especially when people do not know each other well enough. Vojnovic and his military police company were not present the entire time in that area; and naturally, people didn't really know each other well. This is why it was so important to verify everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Page 19, line 5, there are some words missing and I think this is an important area as to orders and tasks and who has to notify whom. That information should be within the transcript. If they could just have the witness re-explain his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you follow that up, please, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Is it page 19, line 5, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you see the mark there indicating words are missing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, the question was: Can the company commander of a military police company receive his orders from any other officer authorised by the brigade commander to issue tasks to the military police company?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brigade commander can authorise another officer to do that, and the company commander can accept such an order. But before proceeding to implement the task, he's duty-bound to verify this with his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If the commander authorizes an officer to carry out a task; for example, to guard prisoners of war, and he -- if he informs of this, the company commander of the military police company securing this, isn't that case the company commander actually implementing this order given by this other officer to guard prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He can do that but only if approved by his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us now turn to the area of responsibility. You must be familiar, as Chief of Staff at the time, that pursuant to the command of the 1st Military District in the entire territory where there was combat, there was an order to establish town commands and to designate town commanders for all sectors where there were no civilian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to these orders, was the town commander duty-bound in accordance with the rules of service, especially those applying to the garrison and barracks service in his area of responsibility to undertake measures and to draft a plan for protecting persons and property for securing -- for ensuring, rather, the control of egress and -- ingress and egress? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order concerning town commanders specified that they were duty-bound to prevent any sabotage and terrorist activity in their area of responsibility to ensure proper transportation, to ensure normal conditions in that area, to prepare conditions necessary for the civilian authorities to function and to assist them in that, and to, in general, be responsible for general security, law an order, in their area of responsibility, rather, in the town where they were town commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And this security pertained both to the security of persons and property?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The order specified that they needed to prevent looting. They needed to ensure physical security to persons, and to provide any other guarantees they needed for peaceful life in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: According to the roles in force at the time, was anybody entering the area of responsibility duty-bound to report to the town commander, and was the town commander duty-bound to inform that person of the roles of conduct which applied in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Such a person had to announce his arrival; and if unable to do so, they had to report as soon as they arrived, and then to proceed with their business that brought them to that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It was up to the town commander to decide whether such a person would be allowed to remain in that area of responsibility or would need to leave?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the person involved. If it was an official person arriving on an official business and if that person arrived from a superior command, then the town commander could not limit his stay there. However, if the person came uninvited, if that's what you have in mind, if this was a person that just wandered in without a specific aim, then the town commander was duty-bound to remove such persons from his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are officers from the superior command duty-bound to report to the town commander when they come to his territory, although they come from a superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Regulations and simply good customs make that necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If there was not a specific task involved -- received from the commander, that is, to stay in the territory of the town command, could the town commander ask such an officer to leave his area of responsibility and to inform his own superior commander about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he can apply that method.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic. Just a few more questions related to the town command. Does the town commander have to know at every moment what is going on in his area of responsibility, that is to say, within the zone of the town where he is commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has to aspire for that. He has to establish a system whereby can be well-informed. He is duty-bound to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will go back to the question of town commands during this examination, because I think this is a very important question for all the parties. And now I would like to start with what I intended to deal with originally. Arriving in Vukovar, you told my learned friend Mr. Lukic about that, and you mentioned some specific characteristics of the Guards Brigade. In addition to that, I would like to ask you something else. In addition to all these special characteristics, what was the multi-ethnic like of the Guards Brigade, in terms of the officers and soldiers there as you were getting ready to go on this assignment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Guards Brigade was a unique brigade in the JNA. Its composition included the best officers, NCOs, and soldiers. The Guards Brigade involves people, and this is something that was really focused on, especially in Tito's time, the people from all republics and provinces should come to the Guards Brigade. Many representatives of all the nations and nationalities, all ethnic groups. So before we went to Vukovar, the brigade consisted of representatives of different nations and nationalities, different ethnic groups. So there were Serbs there, and Croats, and Muslims, and Macedonians and Slovenes. All others as well, not to mention all the 36 ethnic groups that we still have to this day in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that the situation as regards officers and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It was proportionate.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you set out on this assignment, the composition was not changed, a selection had not been made; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we set out on this assignment, there was no special differentiation. Only the battalion for security did not go out on this assignment, and also the guards military orchestra. All other units were involved in our basic task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These units that stayed on in Belgrade that did not go out on this assignment, did they actually stay on to carry out their regular duties, the regular tasks of the Guards Brigade that it otherwise carried out on a daily basis in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These units remained to provide security. That was the battalion for security of facilities and important personages, so its task does not differ in war or in peace, and they continued doing that. Some people stayed from the command structures who were not indispensable for combat tasks. For example, Colonel Janjetovic who was assistant commander for special technical matters and communications and who was now liaising in terms of these tasks and these people who stayed on at the Belgrade garrison. He had his associates there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This unit for security, you said that it provided security for the Federal Secretary and the chief of the General Staff. My question is whether it provided security for the other members of the Presidency of the SFRY as members of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Every members of our Supreme Command, or, rather, member of the then was a member of the Supreme Command, and they had everything that belonged to them as if they were all the President of the Presidency, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So that's the reason why this unit had to stay on in Belgrade, to carry out these functions because the Presidency was functioning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the Federal Secretary was functioning, and everybody else and quite a few other institutions. There wasn't a state of war that was on for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panic. My learned friend Mr. Lukic asked you about the unit's departure for Vukovar, and you said that that was done on the basis of an order issued by the chief of cabinet of the Federal Secretary for National Defence. 403 is the exhibit number, Your Honours. I don't really need it on the screen, but I'm just referring to it. This order resubordinated the Guards Brigade to the 1st Military District while carrying out the assignment at the Vukovar front; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I will be interested in the following: Do you know or do you remember that when arriving at the Vukovar theatre of war, although you were resubordinated to the 1st Military District, through this order, further on through the order of the Military District, were you resubordinated to the 12th corps, or, rather, Operations Group South that was then within that military district?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is such an order. While preparing for this testimony I saw that order so within the 1st Military District, the 12th corps, but that lasted until Colonel Mrksic was appointed commander of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. We are going to get to that moment. Thank you. In your testimony, you mentioned a special characteristic of the Guards Brigade or rather the staff of the Guards Brigade and you were its chief; namely, the existence of a desk officer for the military police battalion. Can you tell me what the tasks were of this desk officer? I assume that you know that because you were his chief; and secondly, did this desk officer go with you to Vukovar, or did he stay on in Belgrade to carry out his duties there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That person was in charge, among other duties, at the operations and teaching organ to be aware of the plan of the military police units, and to make sure that they are properly trained, and to make proposals related at their higher combat readiness, to supervise the situation in these units, and to propose certain solutions to the Chief of Staff and the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did that person go with you to Vukovar, or did that person stay in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the meantime, certain changes took place in the staff. In the meantime, that person was appointed battalion commander; and then as battalion commander, he went to carry out this task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adim Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When he went as battalion commander to carry out his tasks, you no longer had him on the staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That desk officer was not there and quite a few officers were, and we had certain losses, the chief of engineer got killed. And at one moment, I mentioned the reason why we stopped keeping an operations log, because we didn't have enough people in the command. And we made an effort to have more of a presence in the units themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us briefly, if you can, since you were Chief of Staff, what are the main tasks of the Chief of Staff of a brigade, a brigade, in this case, the Guards Brigade, but a brigade in general?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our rules and regulations specify them very concretely, but in the briefest possible terms, the Chief of Staff of a brigade is in charge of the staff. He has organs in the staff, if necessary, I'm going to enumerate them; that's the operations and teaching organ, then the head of arms and services, then the assistant organ that makes it possible to provide logistics and material resources. So the Chief of Staff is in charge of the organs of the staff, takes part in planning, and making decisions, makes proposals to the commander in terms of certain solutions, suggests the use of various units. Quite simply, the Chief of Staff does most of the things at the command; and at the same time, he is the deputy commander of the brigade. If necessary, we can go into greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. For the most part, you have said everything, haven't you? All the duties of the Chief of Staff, you said that he is deputy commander, that means in his absence, right, when the commander is not there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can the Chief of Staff, in keeping with a decision made by the commander, give tasks to subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the commander's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does the Chief of Staff also supervise the implementation of the decisions made by the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, primarily on the ground. So once a decision is made for some tasks, for a combat activity, these tasks are issued to subordinate commanders. The commanders go out to carry out this task or these tasks, and the Chief of Staff, with his organs and personally, supervises the implementation of these tasks, or, rather, how they are put into practice. On that basis, I and some of the organs of the command -- I mean, there were some people who did not find it necessary or -- I don't know, perhaps some people will take offence, but some did not dare go where perhaps at some moment they should have gone. So then some other people happened to be there. I'm referring to myself. I'm not -- I don't think I'm too brave, but my subordinates can say where they saw me, what I was doing, and I'm also referring to the persons present here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, you said that the Chief of Staff, together with the staff, prepares decisions, or, rather, elements that are needed for a commander's decision and makes proposals as to how units should be used. Can you explain this to us in a few sentences?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the situation in the units, on the basis of the situation on the ground, the Chief of Staff with his organs makes a proposal of how units should be used, or, rather, a draft decision for the commander and shows the commander that decision, draft decision. The commander and his assistant commanders can agree with some elements, disagree with others. They can agree with it in it's entirety as well. There are situations when the draft is good, when the commander simply says: "I accept the decision as drafted by the Chief of Staff, and I hereby order that its implementation start." And there are situations that are the complete opposite: "Thank you, chief, but it's going to be different."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand this fully. But it is the duty of the Chief of Staff, taking into account all the circumstances involved, to prepare the decision that is the best possible in their opinion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to provide him full information so that he would make his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So we can say that the Chief of Staff is in charge of the staff that constitutes the basic organ of the brigade command; and, from a functional point of view, it brings together all the organs of the command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. I don't seem to have the transcript on my screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After a decision is made, do the staff and the organs of the brigade elaborate this decision in detail and the use of the unit in terms of that decision? Do they compile the necessary combat documents, and do they transmit this order to subordinate units, or, rather, subordinate commanders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. This is something that is done in all situations where time allows. When a task is urgent, when the situation on the front is such that it requires an urgent intervention, then ordering can be done verbally; and it can go directly, without consulting command organs and without producing the necessary documents. That is to say, within the JNA, ordering could be done both in writing and orally, and both of them had same validity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the supervision of how the order of the commander was implemented was one of the tasks of the Chief of Staff, and that that was the reason why you specifically toured front lines, toured units, to see how the tasks were implemented. Yesterday, you said that you mostly toured the right flank of the disposition of your unit because there were more problems there; did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were other flanks of your combat disposition also toured, and was information collected there as well? Which organ was in charge of this type of supervision?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I toured the left flank also, but less frequently than other units. When I say "left flank," I'm referring to the territory in the area of responsibility of the 1st Assault Detachment. There were a number of officers who were sent to tour that unit as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given that at one point assault detachments were established, did each axis have an officer supervising that particular area, or did that depend on the day, on the task, on the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assault detachment did not have their, if I may say so, permanent mentor. For example, on one day, a chief of engineering could tour them. On another day, chief of signals or chief of atomic, biological, and chemical warfare or quarter master service chief. It just depended on what problems arose in the unit and what assistance they required.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were these officers sent to certain sectors, or did they go there on their own initiative as part of their regular duties?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often, they would receive a task; that is to say, they couldn't simply say: "I'll go and check what's happening there. I want to go and smell the powder, the gun powder." They would normally be given a task to go there; however, there were also situations where a person in charge would make an assessment that it was necessary to go and do something; and, upon completing his task, such a person would normally inform his superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Given that this involved the supervision of the implementation of an order, did you, as Chief of Staff, designate persons who would go and supervise?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If there were members of staff. But I wasn't in the superior position to the entire command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I suppose that assistant commanders went, when necessary, and when, in their own view, they had to do something?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, providing that the commander approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was the 3rd Assault Detachment also supervised, and the anti-terrorist company?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So it wasn't just the left and the right flank but all units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say the right flank, I'm referring to all units all the way up to the Danube in Vucedol; and then the combat disposition of the 3rd Assault Detachment Mitnica, the 80th Brigade, or the 20th Brigade, and the 2nd Assault Detachment and all other units that were in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, given what you told us about how much time you spent outside of the command touring the units, tell us how much did you normally -- how much time did you normally spend at the command? How long you stay?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me first mention that combat operations in Vukovar were quite unique, and they mostly took place during daytime. As soon as it became dark, combat ceased, both on our side and on the side of the paramilitary formations in Vukovar. Somebody observing it from the side could have concluded that it was some kind of a tacit agreement, that we needed to have a break, and then continue on the following day. So in the evening, we would discuss and plan operations for the following day. Now, as to how much time I spent there, well, let me tell you, during daytime, I would be present at the command post very briefly. And after completing tours of units, I would always attend regular briefings, except on several occasions where I happened to stay with the unit after it was dark, and it wasn't advisable to move around after dusk. So as I said, during daytime, I would be present very little. I would normally leave in the morning and come back in the evening; and at night, I was at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We will go back to these issues of the work of the command during night hours, but I think that it's time for our first break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, let us proceed. You spoke about how much time you spent at the brigade command, that there was work regarding the daytime combat operations. Can you tell me, please, how long into the night did the command work, and when would duty officers take over after the rest of the command went to sleep?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the command functions incessantly, 24-hours a day. Depending on the task and the need, a certain number of persons always remained there during the night to do the work. Most often after midnight, there would be duty officers, be it regular organs on duty or reinforced ones. They had the right and authority to call up Chief of Staff or commander at any time, if there was a task or a problem that they couldn't resolve on their own, or if they required the position and opinion of the commander or Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on what you said, the duty organ had to decide whether he could resolve the problem on his own or he needed to wake-up the Chief of Staff or commander or leave the information for the following day to be conveyed then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The events which transpired during duty hours and the documents which arrived during duty hours, were they recorded? Was there a log book of the duty service?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command post in the operations room where most of the work was conducted, there was a war log, a war diary. War diary is the most important document and all relevant events are recorded there, be it day or night. It is recorded continuously.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the sake of the transcript, on page 33, question and answer are written together. The second portion is the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there a log book of the duty officer at the brigade command? In addition to the war diary, was there such a log book?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In addition to the war diary that you mentioned at the command of OG South or command of the Guards Motorised Brigade, was there also a log book of the duty officer, where he recorded all events which transpired during duty service, as well as all documents which arrive during duty hours?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A duty officer normally had his own notebook. In addition to the war diary, another official document was a ledger or a registry book, and the duty officer typically had a notebook where they recorded the tasks received, reports received, and the information conveyed and to whom it was conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So every duty officer had his own notebook?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone had their own official notebooks which were stamped and maintained at the command. There wasn't a special log book for duty service. There wasn't one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a ledger or a registry book. Can you please tell us what kind of information was recorded there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was recorded there were orders received and orders conveyed to subordinate units; reports, reports that were recorded and received, as well as any other documents that were arriving from superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was there a registry book for orders arriving encoded to the command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to the orders arriving in writing, there were also encoded, encrypted orders. And there was a special registry book for such orders; this book was maintained by specialist organs from the signals unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Where were these documents kept, the ones maintained by the signals unit? Was it in their premises or the premises of the command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They kept those documents. And later on, just like all other documents, they were compiled together and handed over to the archives. I know very well that in the building, where the brigade command was during peacetime and where the room was where documents were archived, all of that was destroyed during NATO bombs. Perhaps one day somebody might be able to retrieve these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was a registry book for briefings where information was recorded on regular daily briefings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, there was no such book. Every officer had his own notebook, where he would record the information which pertained to him. This type of book was kept during peacetime; only peacetime, not wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me which command organ was in charge of maintaining the war journal, the ledger, or registry book of the orders that arrived, and who maintained the operations diary? You said that such a diary was maintained only initially

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said so. And I explained why they ceased entering information in the operations log book. As for the ledger or registry book, that was kept by the people working in the office of general administration. At the time, the people there were two warrant officers; one was Radisavljevic, and the second one was Male Bore [phoen], if I'm not mistaken. They were in charge of the ledger. As for the war diary, which was kept at the command post, several people entered information into it; first of all, Trifunovic, Radoje, most of the information was entered by him, then Bratislav Goykovic and Dragan Skoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the operations log book initially?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, it was kept by Trifunovic, Goykovic, and Skoric. They did it in parallel, because they kept two documents in parallel continuously, and because it was necessary to use staff officers in units; and because a number of officers were killed, and so on, because Lukic was sent -- was appointed commander of Assault Detachment and the Vukovar barracks. For all of those reasons, we decided to proceed with just one such document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that here before the Tribunal, a witness said that all these documents were kept until the end of the operation, and that they were safe-guarded after that at the brigade, do you think that that man remembered that properly, and does this jog your memory? Sorry, 8288, lines 11:23 and lines from 7 to 23 on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He can say that and think that, but I stick to what I said. And I think that I got it right. Perhaps I did make some oversights, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, who was responsible to the commander for the accuracy of these entries about the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And who was in charge of safeguarding these documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant Chief of Staff for operations and teaching, at that time, Branislav Lukic; afterwards, it was Trifunovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said, "afterwards, it was Trifunovic," does that mean that that happened after Lukic went to be commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when it was that you last saw these documents when you were at the Guards Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw them when we stored them, when we actually locked them up and sealed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was that after the return of the Guards Brigade in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was upon our return.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After these documents were sealed, you were in charge of safeguarding them at the war room as the Chief of Staff of the Guards Brigade, still; right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assistant Chief of Staff for operations and teaching was in charge of that, but then there's this hierarchy. There's this chain. I was his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you became commander of the Guards Brigade, and when you handed over the duty of Chief of Staff, whose duty was it to safeguard these documents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents remained where they were. When there was this hand-over of duty, one did not do it in terms of individual documents. All documents were dealt with, that is to say, the entire war room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that those who took over the duty of safeguarding the war room did not individually inspect every document; is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So he just received the documents according to a list that was then presented to him, I assume?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily, documents that were in force for the war use of the unit, that is to say, war plans. These documents were received as they were packed and sealed. Quite simply, documents from a period to/from, according to an internal list. He was not duty-bound to inspect the internal list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Among these documents was the war diary there, the operations diary there, and the ledger of orders that arrived, and also the ledger of orders that were coded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are aware of the fact that -- or, rather, that you probably had the opportunity to see the war diary of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: While you testified where you testified, did you see the operations log or this ledger of coded orders?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: They could not hear the witness. Could Mr. Vasic please turn off his microphone when he finishes his questions. There is typing and other background noises. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please be so kind as to repeat your answer? The interpreters did not manage to hear it, because my microphone was on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The war diary, I had occasion to see it. The operations log and the ledger, I saw them considerably later. When I started preparing intensively for this testimony, I saw the copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where it was that you saw the copy of the operations log?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never saw the operations log after the said time. I am sorry, a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to something that has to do with formations that your unit became a part of; that is to say, the Operations Group as an ad hoc formation. I think that yesterday you said that they are usually established at corps or division level; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our principles and regulations, an operations group is a temporary composition, and it is established for carrying out a specific task. Upon the completion of that task, it is disbanded, units go back to their original units. As for all these temporary compositions, in principle, one knows which commands can establish them. In order to be able to plan and supervise combat operations, usually it is the division command or the corps command that is in charge. This is a command that has a certain number of people and that is conceived in a way enabling it to plan activities successfully and command subordinate units. May I say straight away, as Chief of Staff, we did not have that, and that was a major problem for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Actually, when such units are established, it has to do with commanding and issuing tasks to joint units at operations level.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken? You already said what problems your command had, because your command became the command of Operations Group South, apart from regulations that were in force, and I'm interested in the problems. Were they bigger towards the end of the operation when many civilians were leaving and when convoys were being returned because of the commotion in the territory where your unit was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the commander of the Operation Group is not one of these commands; namely, a division command or a corps command, then the officer that establishes an operative group through his order is duty-bound to reinforce the command by persons from other units so that the said command could function. We got, as I mentioned yesterday, only two additional officers, not to repeat their names. And since you mentioned this, we had most of our problems towards the end of the operations; the operation in Vukovar, that is. Because of all of these situations, primarily because of the large number of citizens that required assistance, the large number of units, the large number of units that were surrendering and being disarmed, and so on. In that period, we needed the greatest help of all, and we had our own losses at the time. Some of our officers got killed, some of our officers were wounded. Our command counter were on the decline and our problems were on the rise. That is it in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We are going to talk about the convoys that were passing by there later. But can you tell me from memory or perhaps you know exactly, how many civilians were evacuated between the 18th and the 21st from the territory of Vukovar over those three days.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over 10.000. Our figure was between 10 and 12.000. I don't know whether that's accurate, perhaps there are even more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to go back to the two officers you mentioned. For my learned friends and the Trial Chamber, it is Exhibit 404, Colonel Pavkovic and Colonel Tesic were sent on the basis of that order. Mr. Panic, I'm saying that even they were not a reinforcement to your brigade in terms of assisting the Operations Group, because they were sent on the 29th of September with your command and with your unit that was going to Vukovar, when no one knew that you would become the Operations Group. And their task was actually to supervise your unit on behalf of the cabinet, the staff of the Federal Secretary under whose command you were then; and then later, you were resubordinated to the 1st Military District. So they had this supervisory function and they were supposed to report to the SSNO. Could it please be enlarged? Could the document please be enlarged, the lower part. Yes, thank you. Mr. Panic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You see here, paragraph 4, "Reports, observations, and proposals should be sent to me from time to time, and when necessary."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I see it. I see it. The witness read it out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So is the chief of cabinet, Colonel Vuk Obradovic who signed it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Am I correct when I say that these two officers were not a reinforcement either, but that they were there as supervisory organs when no one knew that you would become Operations Group South?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says that Pavkovic is being sent to the command and Terzic to the artillery command; they were with us from the very outset. At the outset, there was no need for any excessive engagement on their part, but later on you will see, from the documents and from the events concerned, it was very useful that Colonel Pavkovic did part of the work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that they were not engaged; I am just saying that they were not sent in order to reinforce the command of your unit. Tell me, please, as for the command of Operations Group South that was established on the basis of the order of the 1st Military District, that's what you told us yesterday, it included the commander, the Chief of Staff, officers of the staff, and assistant commanders, assistant brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, meetings at the command that you talked about yesterday, you said that they practically took place every day and that they were held around 1800 hours on a given day.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to put something to you, and you probably know about that. These are combat reports sent by the command of Operations Group South that bore a certain date and time, 1800 hours. These were daily reports, 24-hour reports. They actually included reports of subordinate units for that period; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We had another officer testifying here for the Trial Chamber and my colleagues. It is page 8229, lines 13 to 20; namely, that these meetings were held around 1700 hours when they were held in the afternoon, and at 8.00 or -- and that is more logical, if we look at the time in the regular combat reports. And before that, reports had to be heard from subordinate commands. Do you still remember these meetings as being at 1800 hours, or does this jog your memory; namely, that they could have been held around 1700 hours?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well. It was possible, but most of them were held at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Another thing that I'd like to clarify. Yesterday, in response to my learned friend, you said how these briefings, how these meetings at the brigade command went. And you said that usually the commander would speak first about what had happened, he'd present his views, and then others would take the floor. What we have here also is evidence given by a certain witness who said that the briefing went differently; that first, commanders of subordinate units gave their reports, and then members of the staff and assistant commanders. And it was only at the end that the commander would make his decision. So what is your recollection? Does this jog your memory, and what actually happened at the time we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That witness is not mistaken, that is correct. The commander would normally open the meeting, give introductory remarks, say what important events took place during that day, perhaps there was an important order that had arrived or something like that. He would give brief introductory remarks, so the commander would be the first to take the floor. This is a typical custom, anyway. Perhaps I wasn't specific enough. Commander would call the meeting to order, give introductory remarks, give the agenda, and then subordinate commanders, naturally, would give their reports, members of command, and then assistants of the commander who would give certain proposals, suggestions, and so on. Then finally at the end, the commander would give his conclusions, issue orders, and the meeting. So there is no disagreement between what I said and that other witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. This is more clear.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I clarified it, because the commander doesn't brief. He only briefs his own superior; whereas in these briefings, he issues orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: All right. At the time when assault detachments were established, would only commanders of assault detachments attend briefings or also commanders of units which comprised assault detachments?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally, the most superior officer would come, that is to say, commanders of assault detachments; however, there were periods of time where, for example, there were various TO units which comprised assault detachments, in which case where commander of such unit, TO unit would also come to such briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said to Mr. Lukic, yesterday, something about orders, saying that tasks were issued by the commander of OG South; both in writing and orally, and that commander of OG South received both written and verbal orders from his superior command, that of the 1st Military District; correct?
