utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because regulations specify that ordering can be done both in writing and orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This regulation about orders, does it apply to all levels of command and to all units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to all. Because it is best when commander or any superior officer issues a task on the spot. We called that commander reconnaissance. That's how we termed it, and that was precisely the reason why a commander would go to a unit or to a formation and issue a task there. As for the lower levels, there was no need, nor were there preconditions for them to issue orders in writing when they were in their combat disposition and could produce immediate effect on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What remains unclear to me is whether at this higher level of command, after an oral order is issued, was it mandatory to produce a written order, or was the oral order sufficient, say at the level of the 1st Military District?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When an order is issued at such a high level, it can be a verbal one; but most often, there would be a written order coming later. However, the task had to be implemented immediately, without waiting for the written order, say, there was an urgent need and documents needed to be produced and so on. If this involved a minor task, then sometimes no written order followed. For example, we have a situation with the chief of General Staff and his subordinate formations. There's not much correspondence between them. They have telephone and other type of contact. Because if they had to constantly write, they would never leave their offices. I'm now referring to peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that they would speak on the phone. You are now referring to orders issued via phone by the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The reports sent to superior command were sent in writing at the level of the brigade command and up; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said to Mr. Lukic that you knew that security organs also sent their reports to the chief of security department within the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, were you familiar with such reports, you, as Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as Chief of Staff, was not superior to the assistant -- assistant commander for security. I was not familiar with his reports, nor was he duty-bound to familiarise me with them. He was not duty-bound to inform the commander either of the full content of his report. No, he would simply inform him of the necessary portions. Security organ normally deals with a number of issues where, for example, there is a security operation in progress and divulging information about it could, perhaps, jeopardise the entire operation. For those reasons, such reports were partially encrypted or protected. And this was regulated by the rules of service, the rules of service on the work of security organs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We spoke of town commands, and I said we would go back to that issue. You must remember that in early November, pursuant to the order of the 1st Military District, command of OG South designated town commands in the vicinity of Vukovar; whereas in Vukovar, itself, commanders of Assault Detachments became town commanders in the territory under their control; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Each of these town commanders had duties and competencies we described today concerning the security of persons, property, and territory?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the command of OG South appointed as town commanders of Jakubovac, Grabovo, and Ovcara Misevic Slobodan, commander of the 20th partisan brigade; and after he left the area of responsibility on the 18th of November, 1991, they appointed Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Misevic was there until the 18th of November, until that unit left our area of responsibility. From the 18th onwards, it was Lieutenant Colonel Vojnovic. But not only was there the commander of Ovcara, but also Jakubovac and Grabovo. And his subordinate commanders, commanders of artillery battalions were town commanders in that area, (redacted) was one such commander and his subordinates as well. I am not familiar with other names but I'm sure you can look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, that order was introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise but I could not envisage that this name would be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In future, if you are planning to refer this name, then just use pseudonym P014.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not going to mention this name again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You were Chief of Staff of OG South. Can you tell us whether the light artillery division of anti-aircraft defence of the 80th Brigade was ever subordinated to OG South or to the Guards Brigade during your stay in the Vukovar region?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 80th Motorised Brigade, within its composition, had a light artillery battalion of anti-aircraft defence, and this unit was deployed in the Ovcara sector. What you asked -- for some reason, the sound is gone -- no, it's all right now. It's gone again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have problems with the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's fine now. I'm not touching anything. This unit had its area of responsibility in relation to air defence. Air defence is a single system in one area. It is under the control and is guided from one centre. In our case, chief of rocket artillery units of air defence, Lesanovic, produced the plan; and based on his plan and his proposals, an order was issued for single control of air space and air defence. Within that framework, that unit received its area of responsibility for air defence. In that regard, they had something in common with the chief of PVO and brigade command. When it came to all other tasks, primarily disciplinary issues and implementation of tasks, they had nothing to do with the command of OG South. Thus, they were not subordinated to the command of OG South; they had their own commander. They could only carry out the tasks of air defence pursuant to a single signal as it is done in all other armies in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for orders I mentioned earlier pertaining to town commands of Jabukovac, Ovcara and Grabovo, these are exhibits --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the numbers of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, say, could he order this person to appoint him as town commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could the commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade appoint him town commander, as is stated in Exhibit 369?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I spoke too soon. His commander could appoint him town commander. Commander of operations group could not appoint him, because this is the area of responsibility of the 80th Brigade, and he cannot go down to that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If commander of Operations Group were to issue orders to parts of the 80th Motorised Brigade, would it go against the singleness of command, because he would be issuing orders through the command of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not advisable in peacetime, let alone in wartime, because it involves conflict of competencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to Ovcara itself, yesterday, you said in response to my learned friend's question that this is a specific place where there is a farm; however, do you remember that there were some houses there, nevertheless? We heard some testimony here that there were some houses there, that some people lived there. It wasn't only hangars. Does this jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, transcript page 339, lines 18 to 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does this jog your memory, or do you still say that it was only ...

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, it is a pig farm. There are quite a few pig sties there. There are some smaller houses there, too, probably the staff live there; the staff that worked at the farm, or they stayed there while they worked there for 24 hours; then there was an administration building which was dominant there. It's a biggish house. Apart from that, there are a few smaller buildings, auxiliary buildings; then there are a few hangars, like the one that we are talking about, for better, for worse. I didn't go anywhere off the road, so I cannot really confirm whether people lived there. People lived there before these events; but at that time, there weren't any civilians there. I don't remember coming across civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you also talked about the artillery of Operations Group South, and you said that it only operated within the combat zone of the Operations Group; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the allotted zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The commander. Now, the commander, did he issue orders in this zone for the artillery to engage only targets that can be proclaimed military targets?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The use of artillery is a serious task, and it has to be planned properly. Every artillery fire is planned, records are made of it, the number of projectiles is set, and the effects are registered, too. Commanders of the artillery units, who are to carry this out, would get an exact plan of action. And this plan would involve only military targets, or, rather, these are facilities and positions on the ground from where paramilitary formations fired at our units or the civilian population. For example, during the course of a day -- I mean, it happened all the time, regularly, shells falling on Negoslavci and other populated areas. I can say that I remember a few deaths within Negoslavci, itself, where these shells fell. So when we discover where it was that they were firing from, then we would plan our own fire at these facilities, exclusively military targets were engaged. However, paramilitary formations moved from one place to another. They would open fire from Mitnica and then they would go to the water tower and then our fire moved the same way then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Battery commanders, commanders of artillery units received information from the chief of artillery; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He plans fire and; on the basis of the commander's order, he conveys this to them, gives them the necessary coordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that the Vukovar Hospital was not within the area of responsibility of Operations Group South, all the way up to the 19th of November when an order was issued to enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So artillery of OG South did not fire this facility; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vukovar Hospital was on the other side of the Vuka River, on the left bank of the Vuka River. Our boundary was the right bank of the Vuka River. And it's not only that we did not fire there; it was prohibited. As a matter of fact, the commander explicitly prohibited anything from going out of our zone and planned firing. We had a supervisor, if I can put it that way. Colonel Zlatoje Terzic for artillery matters, together with our chief of artillery, he verified the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Zlatoje Terzic is a Colonel, an officer, from the SSNO, from the Supreme Command; right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Kadijevic's order, or rather, his chief of cabinet issued that order sending him to our artillery organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether the artillery of OG South ever targeted wells in Vukovar and the surrounding area during combat operations? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wells?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Wells from where people drank water.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information, but that is impossible. I would really like to see someone manage to hit a well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know that wells were allegedly targeted at moments when people came there to get water? Is that possible? You're an experienced soldier. Is it possible to have that kind of targeted, precise shooting, to make this kind of information reliable?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I considered this to be a pure fantasy. First of all, we are not people like that; and secondly, fire is planned and people move about. We never targeted people. Why would we? I mean, somebody was either joking or speaking just off the top of their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to deal with something that you referred to yesterday, too. You talked about the Croat forces in Vukovar; and as you took different parts of Vukovar, and when the combat operations were over, you talked about booby-traps. What are booby-traps, actually, and how do they work?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the actual combat activities in Vukovar were actually fighting in built-up areas. Fighting in built-up areas is considerably different from fighting in an open space. This is very complex, difficult action, and the outcome is very uncertain. A certain group is established for such actions that would make it possible for them to move up to a particular house or up to a particular street. Sometimes we'd even have to go through a wall in order to avoid a particular area. For example, yards. Yards were mined as a rule. Then gateways, gates were always mined, and entrances, doors to houses. Booby-traps are precisely used in built-up areas. They are supposed to inflict losses and, even more, to have a psychological effect on the other side. Those who want to go that way enter a particular area. So as we went there, we never knew where there would be a booby-trap. You would try to open a door, the doorknob would explode. You tried to entered gate or you tried to turn on the light where there was still electricity at the time, the same thing happens. You lift an object, and they really went to incredible lengths sometimes. Corpses of animals and even human beings were mined. That is contained in many of the records from that period and this, indeed, did happen. That would be it, in the briefest possible terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After combat activities, were there such mines and booby-traps in the centre of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many and for a long time, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I would like to move on to something that is not directly related to what happened in Vukovar, but I am convinced that my learned friends from the Prosecution are going to show you these regulations. So I would like to ask you something about that. Actually, it has to do with Exhibit 396, laws of war. Could we please see this on the screen. Article 1 first. Tell me, as we are waiting to see the document, as an officer, are you aware of this rule on the application of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we insisted on that. As a matter of fact, even soldiers got these handbooks that they carried in their pockets that dealt with that subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You're talking about Vukovar when you went to the Vukovar front? I mean, what you said just now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. Could we see Article 1, please. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: These regulations are referred to here and conditions under which it is implemented. I am just going to read this very slowly and could you please just follow it: "The provisions of these instructions contain principles and rules of international law of war in armed -- in an armed conflict of an international nature and prescribe the way in which these regulations are applied ..." Next page, please. "... in the armed forces of the SFRY, as to say the JNA and Territorial Defence, in an armed conflict in which the SFRY takes part." That's Article 1. Now Article 3. The time when this instruction is applied. "The armed forces of the SFRY shall apply these instructions during the period of time in which the SFRY takes part in an armed conflict. Individual provisions of these instructions will be applied even after the cessation of the armed conflicted if so prescribed by these instructions or specifically ordered." Could I see page -- or rather Article 39 stating when the armed conflict starts. Article 39, page 36. Thank you. It says here: "Beginning of armed conflict. If a state or several states carry out an armed attack against the SFRY or declare war on the SFRY, the SFRY shall, from the moment the armed conflict starts or from the moment of declaration of war, be in a state of lawful self-defence and shall resort to force to repel the attack. From that moment onwards, the SFRY and the state or states that committed an armed attack against it are in a state of armed conflict." "For the SFRY, an armed conflict starts also from the moment when its competent authority informs the United Nations, or rather, the other side in the conflict, that the SFRY takes part in collective armed action of the United Nations against an aggressor. From the beginning of the armed conflict, the parties in conflict are duty-bound to apply rules of international law of war." Mr. Panic, does this mean that these rules are applied in an armed conflict, an international conflict, and in the case of aggression against the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: They did not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness was answering before the matter was even translated to the Prosecution or in English. If this is going to be questions in a legal nature of whether or not this was an international armed conflict, an armed conflict, or whatever type of conflict, that's out of the area of this person who is a fact witness, or a quasi expert on military issues. But if we're getting into issues of the type of conflict that existed and whether or not there were two nations or two states involved, this is outside of his area of observation or expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just read what the rules said. The rules that the witness had to be aware of as an officer. And I'm simply asking him whether the rules say that these rules are applied in case of international conflict. As an officer, he had to know that. I think that this question is proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, I can help you this much: If you ask him what his understanding of this rule was, you can get that much into evidence. But beyond that, Mr. Weiner's objection is well-founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What is your understanding of these provisions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just like anybody else analysing this text, I can see that this pertains to an international conflict where there are two states participating as warring sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are now going to turn to something quite different. Yesterday, you said that in certain -- at a certain time, a commander of the 1st Military District, and even chief of General Staff came to Vukovar, but that you were not part of those events; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on my position, I wasn't duty-bound, nor was I ordered to attend the meetings where these high officials were, but I saw them when they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Certainly, you were Chief of Staff of OG South. I believe that's a position high enough, and that that was not the reason for you not being included in various functions held when they arrived; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not a person who should greet head of the army or chief of General Staff unless my commander is absent. If I am away from the command post doing my task, then naturally, I can't be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I was going to ask you about. Do you remember where you were and what tasks you had during the visit of these high dignitaries?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be traced down in the war diary. I don't remember where I was, but I saw these people. I wasn't part of the delegation they met with. I just had a brief meeting with the commander of the 1st Military District, but not with the chief of the General Staff. Commander of the army, that is to say, commander of the 1st Military District came several times. I was there when he came for the first time. It was then that he defined area of responsibility and OG South and gave specific tasks showing them on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That must have been early October.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now that we are discussing the persons you saw, did you ever see General Aleksandar in Vasiljevic from the 18th to the 21st of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I couldn't tell you what day it was. It was in the afternoon or in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see him just once or more than once during this period?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know definitely I saw him once, but I wouldn't rule out that he came more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you told us that you knew that Seselj came to Vukovar once. Do you know whether commander of OG South during the Vukovar operation objected to any political activity in your area of responsibility? Do you know what his position was on the matter?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Mrksic valued his authority, and if I may be allowed to say so, he was a true commander at the time. I don't want to go into description of his character. But in response to your question, I will tell you that he did not allow anyone to interfere into command, nor did he allow any political influence. The units that were under his command had to carry out the tasks ordered by him. There was no room for any politics or any activity of political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on this, I can put the following question to you: Did any political or party leader come? Could they come during combat operation for a visit? Come to the command, not to the territory itself.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember some situations where there were telephone calls at the command post. People asking for consent, announcing their arrival in the role of advisors; be it retired generals or former soldiers or rather old soldiers from World War II. Be it politicians or people from the government, no one was allowed to come. Commander did not issue his consent for anyone to come to the area of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Arkan here. I think you even mentioned Badza Stojcic, did they ever come to the area where your unit was engaged, up until the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about Arkan from the media. He had quite a high profile. Not once, except for the day when the cabinet session was held, did he come to our area. Had he tried, he would have been arrested in our area. However, on that day when the cabinet session was held, he was a member of the delegation, together with Goran Hadzic and his ministers and as such, he entered the room. Nobody even knew that he was there until we came to the session. If you have time, I can tell you that he went to the units, and he went behind the units where the discipline was loose and where there was room for him. He stood no chance in our area. As for Badzo Stojcic, I only knew about him later on when he was minister of the Interior, but I can tell you that he never visited our area. I know, however, about some of his activities, previously, where he wanted to become famous by attacking a Silo. And we just thought it was a cheap trick.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Goran Hadzic and the government, did they ever come to the area under your control before the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither Goran Hadzic nor the government cabinet. They did function, but it was outside of our area. I think that they had their seat in Dalj. It is possible that some of his ministers visited. I think that one of them frequently came to Negoslavci. He might have been called Bogunovic or something like that. I know we had security issues with him and he was a personae non gratae in our area as well and then he left. I know that Major Sljivancanin had security problems with some people. Until that date, they never functioned as a government, and on that date, they showed up and they said: We are the government. We are in power. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 18th of November, 1991, and the events in Vukovar itself. Can you tell us where you spent that day? You touched upon this yesterday, but can you tell us what tasks you had and where you spent that day.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, the number of persons from paramilitary formations who had crossed over to our territory increased. They provided important information to us. The number of civilians found by us in shelters and basements also increased. They could have crossed over to our territory from where they were. They could see us. We called them, called out to them, but they were not allowed to do that because paramilitary formations used them as a shield. They used them as a sort of a guarantee that we wouldn't open fire on them. This is what happened during the last days of the Vukovar operation. As the 18th approached, it was quite obvious, there were indications that they would surrender at Mitnica, and given how we liberated some key strongholds of theirs, for example, elementary school, high school, even the water tower itself. I was on the axis leading to Vodotaranj. I left from the barracks together with a group of soldiers and officers. If you need some names, I can give you them. And together with units advancing along that axis towards the water tower, we reached the water tower on the 18th in the afternoon after sporadic fighting. There was no fierce resistance there. We placed that territory under our control. And instead of the checkerboard flag which flew over the water tower -- and that represented a huge problem for us throughout the operation, because from that water tower, they would always fire at our soldiers from a sniper. Water tower was built off solid material and it was a dominant feature in that area. And it was important for us to remove the checkerboard flag and hoist the state flag of Yugoslavia which is what we did. That symbolised the liberation of Vukovar and the fact that the main combat ceased. Below the water tower towards Ovcara, in Mitnica region, a unit of 170 men surrendered and we then applied the procedure that was already described here. This was what I have to say in brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you reached the water tower in the afternoon. Was it still daylight?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After hoisting the flag, the Yugoslav tri-colour flag on the water tower, where did you personally go?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the barracks together with the people who were with me, the officers, Savo Cujetinovic, Jovan Susic, Branislav Lukic, and others, Babovic, staff sergeant. We all went to the Vukovar barracks. And as we went back, a huge column of people started following us, people leaving wineries, shelters, basements. All of a sudden these people started following us freely to the barracks, Negoslavci and Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you stay long in the barracks or did you change location and go elsewhere that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't stay there long. I was back at the command post before dark. We talked about how to help these people, how to assist them, what advice to give them, so that's what we dealt with, assistance to civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After the barracks, you say you went to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, even though in one of my previous statements, until I saw some footage and some documents -- you know I gave many statements under different circumstances. And with various psychological problems due to my personal situation, I was misled. And I stated in one of the statements that I went on the 18th towards the hospital, but that is absolutely impossible. Later on when I checked documents and the footage, I realised it was impossible. I remember well that going from the water tower towards the hospital, in one of the streets, I came across a Campagnola, a military vehicle. And there was staff sergeant Devic there and also the wounded and captured sergeant Jovic and the soldiers with him. I'm now correcting my statement saying that that was on the 19th of November and not on the 18th. Because on the 19th, while some persons and some units had tasks relating to the hospital, liberation of hospital, and so on, my task and that of other units, was to sweep the terrain looking for remaining paramilitary formations, mines and explosives, as well as giving advice to the people who had suffered for so long as to where they needed to go. That is to say, that on the 19th, I was by the water tower and then on the 19th in the afternoon, I was also at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic, we will need to break. We will resume at -- we must have a half-hour break because of the redaction. We will resume at five minutes to 1.00. You are watching your time, are you, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I am watching my time. This is a witness who was Chief of Staff so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I expect to finish tomorrow during the course of the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Our inclination is to suggest to you, Mr. Vasic, you should try to finish today. There are two other counsel to deal with this witness. If you would consider that over the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, just before the break, we heard from you that what you said happened on the 18th; namely, your coming to the hospital, that that actually took place on the 19th. On the 18th of November, did you go to the command post in Negoslavci for a briefing?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what the topic of the briefing was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the briefing was attended by all, like until then, the main subject was -- or rather, a task was received from the command of the 1st Military District for the further clean-up of Vukovar, the liberation of the hospital, and taking care of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At that meeting, was any reference made to evacuating the hospital, and were tasks related to evacuation handed out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The liberation of the hospital was discussed, further activities aimed at liberating the hospital. As for tasks related to evacuation of the hospital, as far as I can remember, they were handed out on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you gave the investigator of the OTP a statement on the 25th and 26th of July and on the 1st of September, 2005?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that you said in this statement that on the 18th of November, 1991, the briefing held at the command in Negoslavci was where tasks were handed out for the evacuation and that the commander did that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly that's what I said. If that's what's written there, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you have the copies that were handed out yesterday of the statements that you gave?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got them here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have an extra copy or he could use our copy. We have our own. It's also on the e-court system if...

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page we need bears the ERN number 04618195 in B/C/S; otherwise, that is paragraph 69. I assume that it's paragraph 69 in the English version, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Does it say here: "Mrksic also informed us at the command briefing in Negoslavci on the 18th of November, 1991, that Major Sljivancanin was going to be in charge of that is command," it says in brackets, "the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th and the 20th of November, 1991. Mrksic said that Sljivancanin was allowed to use as many military policemen as necessary to escort the prisoners and ensure their safe passage. If I remember correctly, Paunovic's military police battalion (that is the 2nd Military Police Battalion) and a company of armoured combat vehicles of the 1st Military Police Battalion were tasked with escorting the prisoners to Sremska Mitrovica." Do you remember having stated something like that to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I stated that, but I kindly ask -- well, perhaps there are some mistakes in some dates and some formulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you read the statement before you signed it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On page 28. If you don't mind, could you look at page 28? There is an acknowledgment that -- stating that it contains everything you said and that that was stated to the best of your recollection and memory. Do you remember whether such a briefing was held on the 18th of November? Was that correct what you said to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The briefing was held. The tasks were given, but I still think it was the 19th. I have a problem with dates, because of my memory. But if possible -- well, it's probably in the war diary, too, noted down in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I haven't found it in the war diary.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I think after having read a series of documents. After refreshing my memory of these events, I think that these tasks were handed out on the 19th. Because I had this mistake, I had this misconception in terms of going to the hospital. It wasn't on the 18th. It was on the 19th, and there is material evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to look at paragraph 66 of that same statement of yours. It's at the end of the previous page. Over here, you are saying who attended the session -- no, not the session, who attended the briefing in Negoslavci. Here you say, "On the 18th of November, 1991," now that you say perhaps it's the 19th. Tell me, I'll read it out and you will tell me whether you remember. "I first heard of the evacuation of the Vukovar Hospital," here it says "on the 18th he have November, 1991, at the daily command briefing of the OG South command in Negoslavci. I believe the following persons were in attendance: Colonel Mrksic, Mile; Major Veselin Sljivancanin; Major Borivoje Tesic, the commander of the 1st Assault Detachment; Major Lukic, commander of the 2nd Assault Detachment; Major Milorad Stupar, commander of the 3rd Assault Detachment; Captain First Class Jovan Susic, commander of the 1st Military Police Battalion; Captain First Class Radoje Paunovic, commander of the 2nd Military Police Battalion; Colonel Milorad Vojnovic, commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, and so on." Are these the attendees on the 19th of November as you say now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to correct myself, the 19th. And in addition to these people, the assistant commanders were there as well. I could give their names, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Logistics assistant Borisa Jurcic; assistant for Morale, Marko Maric; then -- well, there. I know for sure about the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you've said, Mr. Panic, it seems that you have less problems with people and more problems with dates.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state at that time to the investigators of the OTP -- please look at paragraph 72 -- I quote: "It was unusual for a security officer to be given responsibility for an evacuation operation. However, I assume Mrksic appointed Major Sljivancanin because of the important role of the security organ in that operation. Sljivancanin was not responsible only for the selection of prisoners; he commanded the entire evacuation of people to Sremska Mitrovica. This implied that Sljivancanin was able to issue orders to the military police or any other unit participating in the operation." Do you remember whether this is what you stated to the investigators of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stated this but, let me tell you, when one reads this statement of mine, the questions are not there. It's not that I am looking for any kind of excuse now, but only if you were to compare questions and answers could you perhaps get the right picture, the real picture. I think that here, perhaps I spoke in haste, or perhaps I was led in terms of phrasing this answer. However, it is a fact that Major Sljivancanin was given the task of selecting -- well, not only he, but with his organs, Dr. Vesna Bosanac, the staff of the hospital, the organs from the security administration who came, to separate combatants from non-combatants. It says here that he is responsible for this group that is supposed to go to Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, what was this important role of the security organs that you referred to here?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had the task since, according to the information we had received, there were armed people in the hospital, too; that there were many members of the paramilitary formations there who did not want to surrender their weapons on the 18th, when that group from Mitnica surrendered. Because this formation from Mitnica far more numerous, a number came out and surrendered. That is one direction of movement. The other direction of movement of their combatants was towards the hospital. They entered the hospital and they tried to disguise themselves. We had that information and that was very important to carry out this selection then in terms of combatants and non-combatants. That makes the role of the security organs so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it because of that important role that the security administration sent its own team separately to carry out the triage of prisoners and the sending out of prisoners of war in the 1st Military District, or rather, the security department of the 1st Military District? Did they send their own people, then, to carry out this selection and triage?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, because this is a difficult responsible complex task, we did not have enough professional people to carry this out properly. So the security administration deemed it necessary to send people, and a group like that arrived. Most of them were experienced people with the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether, at the time of the evacuations in Vukovar, the ones that you mentioned, including this evacuation of the hospital, do you know that the command of the 1st Military District set up some commission that was following the course of these evacuations and sending reports to the command of the 1st Military District in terms of how the evacuations were taking place?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that, and there are documents following that activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: For a moment, I'd like to go back to documents related to the evacuation, or rather, orders. Yesterday, you said that you did not see any written documents. There is this one that was shown to you by the investigators of the OTP. I'm going to ask you now; this is the document, or rather, the order. It is Exhibit 415. It's strictly confidential document 161482/81, and you have it as number 43. Please take a look in the statement that you gave to the OTP; it is paragraph 43.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this document, in paragraph 1 it says that Operations Group South is going to carry out detailed full preparations; and in concert with Technical Group North during the course of the morning on the 19th of November, take the hospital MUP and clean the liberated parts of town from remaining Ustasha groups. This is the only order that actually authorises Operations Group South, that after the 18th of November or rather on the 19th, they cross the Vuka River and go to the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The hospital was outside our area of responsibility. Up until the 18th, no one had crossed the Vuka River. The task that we got was for the 19th to liberate the hospital. Until 1000 hours, we carried out task at 11.00, and there are written documents confirming that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind these provisions and the evacuation of the hospital, does it not seem to you that there must have been a written order of the command of the 1st Military District. And that its number should be 161482/82?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Triage selection and evacuation of the hospital is a serious task. The 1st Military District was supposed to take active part in this and spell out in its own order the duties of individual persons and organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that considerable logistics were involved, Jelko Crmaric was there, assistant commander for logistics of the 1st Military District. Do you remember that perhaps there was such an order there at the time and now at least I did not manage to find it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that among those documents, there was one. I believe there was one. And how come it has gone, I don't know. I know that Jelko Crmaric, now that you mention him. He also came to our command post as logistics officer. He had duties and tasks to support, first of all, the transportation, or rather, the logistical part of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Due to the fact that we're running out of time, let me try it this way: Would you please look at paragraph 43 of Exhibit 415. OTP investigators asked you about paragraph 5 and paragraph 8, which is resolute prevention of non-military conduct and wilful conduct by certain local TO units.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that, "This was not consistent with the situation in our zone of responsibility. They probably referred to TO units in the zone of responsibility of OG north, not the TO detachment Leva Supoderica of Petrova Gora. We understood this order as a warning by the 1st Military District commander, who wanted to draw our attention to the matter and prevent the occurrence of similar incidents involving local Serbian TO members in our zone of responsibility. I believe that Colonel Mile Mrksic, as a result of this order by the 1st Military District, issued a similar order to our subordinated units asking them to prevent in our area of responsibility the occurrence of such incidents as described in paragraphs 5 and 8." Did you state this to the OTP investigators, and is this true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and a brief comment. The 1st Military District wrote an order of this nature based on the information in some other units. However, it is a regular practice that if something happens elsewhere, other units are warned of this as well. And this is why this order was sent to us. You can see, based on this order, to whom it was forwarded, which is not to say that events described here occurred in all of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, please tell me in relation to this evacuation, and this is something you said to Mr. Lukic yesterday. You had no knowledge of the Zagreb Agreement at the time in November of 1991. While you were in Vukovar, you didn't know that there were negotiations held in Zagreb or what the outcome was; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew that there were constantly some negotiations held, that there were contacts. General Raseta was in Zagreb, so there was constantly something going on on the diplomatic scene. Frequently, we received orders on cessation of hostilities which we abided by. But the opposing side would very soon violate them. Based on that, I know that the negotiations activity was quite intense, but I didn't know about the outcome. When preparing for this testimony, I learned that there was such a document, but I didn't know it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit 419 now, which is dated 19th of November, order of the command of OG South. Could we please zoom in on the first portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Mr. Panic, can you see this? This is dated the 20th of November, 439-11, strictly confidential, regulation of daily activities. Could we see the second paragraph: "In parallel with this, conduct evacuation and transport of civilian population, the wounded, and sick from the hospital in Vukovar." Is that what it says there, and would you agree with me that no crime suspects are mentioned here nobody suspected of committing war crimes participating in armed rebellion is mentioned here. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thus, by means of this document, a commander of OG South orders the following persons be evacuated. Would you please look at paragraph, above item, 4 which begins with the words: "Town commanders." "Town commanders in area of responsibility of OG South shall take all measures necessary for full functioning of military authority in accordance with the order strictly confidential number 349-1 dated 9th of November, 1991." Is this a warning of the commander to town commanders, asking that they ensure everything necessary for the functioning of military authorities and protection of persons and property in their area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was one of the written orders, in addition to numerous verbal orders, that accompanied any contact with subordinate formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us turn to the portion concerning the Mitnica group. You said that they surrendered, that they were taken to Ovcara, where they were guarded by the military police of the 80th Motorised Brigade. Do you know whether the command of OG South, Colonel Mrksic, ordered commander of the 80th Motorised Brigade, before the 18th of November, to locate in his area of responsibility an appropriate facility where a temporary detention centre could be established for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the surrender was expected, there were proper preparations and the command of the 80th received such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did the commander of the 80th inform, then, the commander of OG South that he had found a hangar at Ovcara, that it was in pretty good shape, and that prisoners could be kept there for a brief period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's how the task was implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know when this group of prisoners of war went to Mitnica from Sremska Mitrovica? Did the military police of OG South provide security to this convoy, or was it the representatives of prison in Sremska Mitrovica, those who came to take over prisoners of war. Did they come to your sector, or rather, to the sector of the 80th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police of the 80th Brigade provided security, provided guards for the hangar. As far as I know, that convoy was escorted by the police of OG South, that is to say, the Guards Brigade, as far as I'm aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before the convoy from Ovcara set out, did the representatives of the prison in Sremska Mitrovica come or not? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now see Exhibit 442, please, which is an order from the same period of time, the 19th of November, of the command of the 1st Military District, strictly confidential, 2346-2, signed by Lieutenant Colonel Vladimir Stojanovic. And it has to do with the prisoners of war and a ban on the exchange of the captured members of armed forces of SFRY for the captured members of Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was sent to me and to the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this would indicate that the decisions on the exchange of prisoners of war fell under the competence of the commander of the 1st Military District, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 19th of November, please tell us. You tell us that you went to the briefing in the evening; you told us all about it. Can you tell us, in the course of the day, what were your movements, but briefly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th of November was the day when we continued clearing the terrain from the remaining groups of paramilitary formations in the territory of Vukovar. In addition to that, the hospital was liberated. I myself, was in the central part of Vukovar on the axis Negoslavci, the barracks, water tower. I was together with the commanders on that axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there? When did you reach the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That lasted until the afternoon hours, that is to say, it was until daylight. I can't give you the exact hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us, yesterday, whom you found in front of the hospital. Did you enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who did you enter the hospital with, and which rooms did you visit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered with two officers. I believe that one was Stanko Mijatovic, and the other one was either Susic or Tesic. I can't be sure. Perhaps they remember. We saw several rooms in the hospital, and we saw that all spaces were used up. The hospital adapted its work to the wartime conditions. They had improvised beds. The fact is that the hospital was completely full. They had some lighting; I think it was powered by a generator. The light was dimmed. And if I were to describe those who were lying, I can tell you straight away that I realised that they were not patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see Vesna Bosanac before you entered the hospital or inside?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She stood at the entrance to the hospital with some other doctors. There were people there with the Red Cross symbols; and Major Sljivancanin was there, and some other officers of ours whose names I couldn't really give you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you saw Mrs. Bosanac, had she already completed her conversation with Colonel Mrksic on not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that she had already had contact with Colonel Mrksic, but he would be better placed to tell you that or other people who were involved in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We heard that from her, too. But I'd like to know who told you that she had already seen Mrksic, or did you learn about this later?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this later, upon my return to the command post. I learned that she had gone there and that she had a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, how long did you stay there at the hospital, and where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed at the hospital for half an hour, at the most, maybe less than that; and then I went back to Negoslavci to the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I suppose that after that, you attended the briefing that you described?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please tell us, until the 19th, when that briefing took place, until what time did you stay at the command post?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that on the 19th, I was at the command post, throughout, the whole time after the briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember until what time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Continuously until the following day, until the following tasks were issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you went to bed, if you remember, roughly?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. Probably later at night. Sometimes we even didn't sleep. It's been too long a time for me to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this group of officers from the security administration, the colonels and others that you mentioned, arrived at the command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that they arrived, but I didn't meet them and I didn't know any of them. It was only later that I saw and learned of some of them, such as Bogdan Vujic, Kijanovic, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you didn't see them personally at the command that night?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the following day, the 20th of November, when did you leave the command in Negoslavci, and where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was around 8.00. I went to Negoslavci because we had sent off a group to Belgrade from the command post. I went to the barracks, and I've already told you about this. Some other assistants of commanders and I had to do something; and later on, Major Sljivancanin got involved, too. Our job was to organise a press conference; that is to say that that morning I went to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was Susic, commander of the 1st Battalion of the military police, present there at the barracks when you came?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how long did you stay in the barracks on that occasion when you came in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed in the barracks -- no, there is a mistake here. I have to make a correction. I really have a problem with the dates, times. There are much too many details, so please allow me to make a correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG PANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day -- it wasn't on that day that the delegation left for Belgrade; that was on the 20th. The --, or rather, that was the 20th and the delegation left on the 21st. I received an order by telephone from Colonel Mrksic. I was told to go attend a cabinet session, and that was sometime 9.30 or 10.00, as far as I can remember. So it was in the morning. Later on, I explained it here. That was the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I spoke to Mr. Borovic and he said that he needed ten to 15 minutes. I would require additional half an hour to conclude my cross-examination, by your leave. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have no objection. It's an important witness. On behalf of the Prosecution, we're not asking for any restriction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Between you and Mr. Borovic, the first half of the first session tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I indicate, as we rise, that at a convenient time, if not earlier at the end of the evidence of this witness, the Chamber would like to receive very brief submissions as to the time parties would need for their final written submissions, and the time when they would be ready, the time that can be expected. With respect to oral submissions, the time that the parties would be ready for those and how long would be asked. These, I think, should be prepared on the anticipation that we will finish Mr. Lukic's case in the time he has estimated, that is by the 6th of December. It's a question of how we set a programme up after that, because we've now seen enough of Mr. Lukic's case to get an idea of the time. And it's in light of that that we will be able to look at the question of when we should sit and when we should not be sitting over the Christmas period. We will adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 10th day of November, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.48 p.m.,
